A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original teacher–student experiments measuring losses, weight spectra, alignments, and optimizer-update norms, including extensive appendix experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original teacher–student results and adds long-training experiments, activation-matching experiments, and VGG11 weight-spectrum results from training on MNIST.

M1.justification: The two-stage procedure, GD/FB-Adam update equations, ridge regression, and optional weight normalization are retained. The VGG11 and activation experiments extend the experimental settings without introducing a new proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: v1 uses synthetic Gaussian single-index regression data throughout. v2 adds actual VGG11 training on MNIST images in Appendix E.6, substantially extending coverage beyond the synthetic domain, although it reports spectra rather than classification performance.

E2.justification: The core GD-versus-FB-Adam comparisons remain unchanged. Auxiliary scheduler comparisons narrow: v1 Figure 35 evaluates CosineAnnealingLR with FB-Adam and weight normalization, whereas v2 Appendix E.4 retains constant-rate and StepLR cases but omits cosine annealing.

E3.justification: v2 adds learning-rate-by-training-duration grids reaching 10,000 updates, a matched tanh/tanh teacher–student control, and VGG11 training for 10 full-batch epochs at learning rate 0.01. The shared one-step and 10-step synthetic comparisons retain their sample sizes, splits, and metrics.

E4.justification: Tables 1, 3, and 4 test whether prolonged training compensates for small learning rates; Appendix E.5 tests dependence on teacher–student activation mismatch. Several earlier diagnostics disappear, including unnormalized 64-step spectra, some 100-step cases, weight-normalized overlap plots, and cosine-scheduler analysis. Most sample-size, noise, and regularization analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations over five runs for the corresponding one-step and 10-step sweeps. No changed run counts, new significance tests, or new uncertainty-estimation procedures are specified.

E6.justification: v2 adds long-duration spectral trajectories, including no heavy-tail emergence at FB-Adam learning rate 0.01 through 10,000 steps, matched-activation loss/alignment results, and VGG11 layer spectra. Several earlier supplementary result entries are removed. Figure 3 and v1 Figure 7/v2 Figure 5 retain their plotted results; the additions do not establish same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1, its assumptions, and the learning-rate corollaries remain unchanged. In Proposition B.6's proof, v2 corrects Equation (33)'s ambient space from R^n to R^(nd+n) and removes the assertion connecting C1 regularity to absolute continuity.

C1.justification: The central claim that heavy-tailed spectra can emerge without stochastic gradient noise is retained. v2 explicitly elevates first-step feature learning and spike formation to a necessary condition for subsequent heavy tails and adds first-work positioning for gradient-noise-free, discrete-step ESD analysis.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the initial spectral gap as affecting the time to heavy-tail emergence and adds substantive activation-dependent qualifications to the generalization relationship. It expands discussion of extreme tail exponents, fitting sensitivity, and applicability to deeper networks. Existing sample-size, regularization, and label-noise interpretations largely move to Appendix E.4.

D1.justification: v2 documents the VGG11/MNIST recipe, including full-batch Adam, learning rate 0.01, and 10 epochs. It removes the omitted cosine experiment's schedule parameters. Existing synthetic defaults and the code-access link are retained; no new hardware or runtime information is supplied.

R1.justification: Sections 1–2 substantially reposition the work against limiting weight-distribution analyses and emphasize discrete-step ESD evolution. Added literature includes heavy-tailed random matrices, compressibility, federated learning, and deeper-network feature learning. The earlier overparameterization/interpolation discussion and several random-feature references are removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and concluding discussion are extensively rewritten. Section 5 is reorganized around spectral transitions, generalization, then singular-vector alignments; sensitivity discussions move into the appendix, and future work becomes an expanded subsection.

P2.justification: v2 adds spectral grids and new transition, activation, and VGG11 figures; combines retained overlap panels into Figure 6; and moves v1 Figure 8 to Figure 27. Several panels disappear. Figure 2c reuses v1's appendix example at learning rate 1, while its accompanying prose still refers to 0.1.

improvement.justification: The 10,000-step controls strengthen the learning-rate evidence, and the matched-activation study usefully qualifies the generalization claims. MNIST provides a limited real-data check, and the proof correction improves precision. The net gain is modest: practical validation remains qualitative, the stronger necessity claim rests on finite empirical tests, several auxiliary diagnostics are removed, and Figure 2c introduces a learning-rate mismatch with the prose.
